description: DBSCAN groups points into clusters by density. A point with enough neighbors within a set radius is a core point. Linked core points form a cluster, nearby points join it, and the rest are noise. FlashLib rewrites classical machine-learning operators like this as fast GPU kernels. ¶ The problem removes the authors’ fast DBSCAN and leaves a plain, slow version. The agent writes a fast GPU version. It must count neighbors, find core points, link them into clusters, and label border points and noise. ¶ It runs on point clouds of 20,000 points in 8 or 32 dimensions, plus hidden cases, one of 200,000 points. To pass, each workload must run faster than the human reference. Its match to the plain version’s clusters and noise must be no worse than theirs.

IVF-PQ is a standard index for nearest-neighbor search over many vectors. It splits the vectors into thousands of lists and compresses each into 16 short codes. A query scans only its nearest lists and estimates distances with table lookups. ¶ This problem leaves only a slow, simple search over a fixed index. The agent writes the fast GPU search. It must pick the lists to probe, build each query’s distance table, scan the codes and keep the k best. ¶ Each submission searches the SIFT image-descriptor benchmark with batches of thousands of queries. To pass, it must beat the human reference on search time for every workload. Its recall must be no lower, both against a full scan and for the true nearest neighbor.

K-means groups points around K centers. Each Lloyd step sends every point to its nearest center. It then moves each center to the mean of its points. Flash-KMeans makes this exact step fast and memory-efficient on a GPU. ¶ The problem replaces the authors’ optimized step with a plain version. The agent writes the step: find each point’s nearest center, then compute the new centers. Results must be exact and repeatable, and an empty cluster keeps its old center. ¶ The test runs two Lloyd steps on six data shapes, two of them hidden. To pass, it must be faster than the human reference on every shape. Its clustering cost must stay within 5 percent of theirs. Almost no extra points may miss their nearest center.

Brute-force k-nearest-neighbor search compares each query vector with every database vector and keeps the k closest. A thousand queries against half a million vectors means half a billion distances per call. FlashLib applies the ideas behind fast GPU attention kernels to classical operators like this one. ¶ The problem removes the fast search. What remains fills the whole distance table, then picks the k smallest per row. The agent writes the search as GPU code, returning each query’s k nearest rows and their distances. ¶ Each submission searches SIFT and GIST image descriptors, with k from 10 to 256. To pass, on every workload it must be faster than the human reference and find at least as many true neighbors. Its distances must match a direct recomputation.

Learning with errors is the hard problem beneath much post-quantum cryptography. Given a matrix A and b = As + e mod q, one must find the secret s. Both s and the error e are small. Extra structure, such as sparse matrices or secrets with few nonzero entries, can open shortcuts. ¶ Here there is no solver to restore. The agent writes its own attacks, such as lattice reduction, and submits one secret per instance. Any secret that meets the published conditions counts. ¶ There are 200 public instances in ten families of matrix and secret structure. Each secret is checked directly: it must use the allowed values, and b − As must be small enough. The human reference submits no secrets, so passing means solving all 200.

Olmo Hybrid, arXiv 2604.03444, motivates the 3:1 Gated DeltaNet reference architecture. The repository ships a locked training and evaluation harness plus reference.py. The agent submits one file, /app/model.py, defining build_model or a NanoSLM class under a 400M parameter cap, optionally declaring a BLOCK_SIZE for training. The judge trains the model from scratch for 900 seconds on one H100 over FineWeb-Edu with the dolma2 tokenizer and measures held-out bits per byte at context 8192. Score is 100 times 2 to the power of minus gamma times val_bpb, normalized so the reference hybrid scores 70, as config.yaml states.

Nano World Models, arXiv 2605.23993, releases a diffusion-forcing video predictor whose Figure 6 shows DDIM step count trading against rollout quality on CSGO. The repository holds a clean checkout at /app/nano-world-model with the frozen NanoWM-L/2 checkpoint. The agent submits a Python-only patch at /app/solution.patch limited to src/diffusion/**.py and src/sample/sampling_utils.py. The judge generates 50 future frames from 4 context images at nominal 50 DDIM steps on hidden episodes on a Modal H100 and measures wall-clock plus LPIPS. Score is clip of 100 log2 speedup times a quality multiplier that stays 1.0 within 3 percent LPIPS tolerance, per the readme, reference 1.17x.

Nano World Models, arXiv 2605.23993, reports that long autoregressive rollouts drift into states that look plausible and are wrong, its Finding 5. The repository holds the same checkout and frozen NanoWM-L/2 CSGO checkpoint. The agent submits a Python-only patch at /app/solution.patch within src/diffusion/**.py and src/sample/sampling_utils.py. The judge runs a long sequential rollout at 50 DDIM steps on a Modal H100 with a horizon drawn per scored run, measures mean LPIPS over the final 20 tail frames, and holds generation time within 10 percent of baseline. Score is 100 times the relative tail-drift reduction times a wall-clock multiplier, per the readme, reference 6.8 percent.

Continuum, arXiv 2511.02230, schedules multi-turn agent requests with job-level FCFS and KV-cache time-to-live so a conversation keeps its prefix resident. The repository holds a pinned upstream vLLM v0.11.0 checkout at /app/vllm. The agent submits a Python-only patch at /app/solution.patch allowlisted to vllm/v1/core/**, vllm/config/scheduler.py, vllm/config/cache.py, and narrow engine, worker, and OpenAI-entrypoint wiring files. The judge serves Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct on one Modal H100 under Poisson arrivals of mini-swe-agent SWE-bench Lite and BFCL memory conversations, gating on greedy token match and per-sample correctness. Score blends clip of 100 log2 geomean latency speedup at weights 0.8 and 0.2 per config.yaml, times an accuracy multiplier.

SCOPE counts small patterns, such as triangles or short paths, around every vertex of a large graph. For each vertex, it reports how many copies of a pattern touch it at one chosen position. Such counts serve as features for graph learning and anomaly detection. ¶ This problem removes SCOPE’s batch mode, which counts many patterns in one run with shared plans. The agent writes it. It must plan the batch, reuse work the patterns share, and output every count. ¶ Each submission counts two batches of patterns on three real graphs: web pages, movie ratings and yeast proteins. Every count must match an independent count exactly. To pass, it must beat the human reference on running time for every graph and batch, in every timing round.

Seer speeds up Ethereum block execution by predicting which way smart-contract branches will go. Many branches test state that earlier transactions wrote. Seer runs each transaction ahead of time and records its path and the state it touches. The real run then draws on these records. ¶ The problem removes the branch predictor. The agent writes it: one small predictor per branch, which answers taken, not taken or unsure. Once the branch runs, the predictor learns from the direction it really took. ¶ It is tested on 600 consecutive blocks of real Ethereum history, split into three periods. Transactions are grouped as complex or normal. To pass, it must beat the human reference on branch accuracy in every period and group. It must also predict whole transaction paths at least as well.

Spectrum runs Ethereum smart-contract transactions in parallel, yet commits them in the order consensus fixed. When two transactions conflict, it does not restart the later one from scratch. It rolls that transaction back to a checkpoint taken partway through and runs on from there. ¶ A checkpoint saves where the program is and every value on its operand stack. This problem removes the stack that makes these checkpoints cheap. The agent writes it: save a checkpoint, restore one, and keep many alive at once without any of them changing another. ¶ Each submission must first restore thousands of checkpoints exactly, checked against a simple reference. It then runs three standard transaction workloads: YCSB, SmallBank and a TPC-C-style order mix. To pass, it must beat the human reference on four counts: throughput, checkpoint creation time, checkpoint restore time and memory per checkpoint.

ScaleGPM estimates how often a small pattern, such as a triangle, occurs in a large graph. It has two engines that meet the same error target. Sampling estimates the count from local neighborhoods. Sparsification keeps a random, color-based subset of edges and counts exactly there. Which is faster depends on the graph and settings. ¶ The problem removes the step that picks between them, and the agent writes it. It sees the graph’s size, triangle count and maximum degree. It also sees the pattern, the error target, both engines’ settings and the core count. ¶ It is tested on 112 settings over eight graphs shaped like social networks. To pass, its picks must run faster than the human reference, in geometric mean, for triangles and for 4-cliques.

Plans built from two-way joins can produce intermediate results far larger than the final answer. The Yannakakis algorithm avoids this for acyclic joins. It first drops rows that cannot match, using semijoins, then joins the rest. ¶ This system turns an optimizer’s binary join tree into such a two-phase plan, but only trees of one shape convert. The problem removes the rewrite that reshapes the tree, and the agent writes it. The new tree keeps the same tables and join keys. Each join’s keys must appear in the leftmost table on both sides. ¶ The plans come from three benchmarks over Stack Overflow, IMDB movie and graph data. Every query must return exactly the original result. To pass, each of the 39 queries must run faster than with the human reference.

Video diffusion models spend much of their time in attention. Sparse VideoGen clusters similar tokens and computes attention only for the cluster pairs that matter. SVG-EAR estimates the skipped pairs from cluster averages and picks pairs by the error skipping would cause. ¶ The problem removes this attention layer and three of its routines, and the agent writes all four. One averages each cluster. One picks which cluster pairs to compute. One computes them and estimates the rest. ¶ The model is Wan 2.1, making 81-frame 720p clips from four prompts. Each clip is compared with the one full attention makes. To pass, every clip must be at least 4% faster than with the human reference. Its PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS image scores must stay within small margins of theirs.

BABBLE learns a library of functions from a corpus of related programs. Rewriting the programs to call these functions makes the corpus smaller. BABBLE keeps the programs in an e-graph, which holds many equivalent forms of each expression. ¶ The problem removes the step that proposes candidate functions. The authors find them by anti-unification: line up two fragments and put a hole wherever they differ. They do this across the whole e-graph, by crossing its tree automaton with itself. The agent writes this crossing and the candidate search. ¶ Each submission learns libraries for corpora from five domains, such as lists, logo drawings and block towers. To pass, on every corpus it must shrink the programs at least as much as the human reference, and run faster.

Szalinski shrinks unstructured CSG expressions into editable CAD programs with map and fold operators using equality saturation and inverse transformations, a way to speculatively add equivalences to an e-graph. The Rust repository defines the Caddy language in cad.rs and holds the rewrite rules, solver, and permutation logic that drive the search. The task deletes the inverse-transformation and rewrite core that produces smaller equivalent programs. The agent reimplements this search so structured programs fall out of saturation. The objective is to match or beat the authors on program-size reduction and wall-clock time across the CAD models the paper reports.

Polygon looks for a small database on which two SQL queries give different results. Such a database proves the queries are not equivalent. It encodes both queries as formulas over tables of a few symbolic rows, and asks an SMT solver for values. ¶ The problem removes Polygon’s search. Polygon never encodes every behavior at once. It commits to some choices and solves that smaller formula. On failure it learns which choices conflict, backs off and widens. The agent writes this loop, end to end. ¶ Each submission refutes 16 wrong LeetCode answers and splits sets of 50 or 100 queries into two equal groups. To pass, it must succeed wherever the human reference does, at most a fifth slower. On two hard pairs it must be over twice as fast.

An e-graph stores many equivalent expressions by grouping them into classes. Equality saturation grows it with rewrite rules, then extracts the cheapest expression. egg’s key idea is to repair the e-graph’s invariants once per batch of rewrites, not after every merge. ¶ This problem removes that rebuild step, and the agent writes it. It must process the pending merges and give every node canonical class ids. Nodes that became identical must merge, and analysis data must flow up to parents. ¶ Each submission runs arithmetic tests from egg’s suite, from differentiation to simplification. Every test must pass, and the invariants are checked separately. To pass, it must beat the human reference by at least 5 percent on every test. That holds for total time and for time spent merging and rebuilding.

Ruler infers rewrite rules automatically by enumerating terms into an e-graph, forming candidate equalities, and filtering to a small general ruleset using equality saturation and characteristic vectors. The under-1000-line Rust implementation runs this enumerate, generate, and shrink loop across booleans, bitvectors, and rationals, validating by model checking, SMT, or fuzzing. The task deletes the candidate-generation and rule-selection core. The agent reimplements characteristic-vector matching and derivability-based filtering. The objective is to match or beat the authors, whose rulesets run 25 times faster to synthesize and 5.8 times smaller than the CVC4 baseline at equal proving power.

This work simplifies Mixed Boolean Arithmetic expressions by holding semantically equivalent forms in an e-graph and rewriting toward simpler terms. The implementation uses the egg equality-saturation library to represent and search obfuscated expressions. The task removes the rewrite-and-extract core that recovers a simplified expression from the saturated graph. The agent reimplements the rewrite rules and extraction so deobfuscation still succeeds. The objective is to match or beat the authors on success rate, simplification ratio, and per-expression time across the Tigress, Qsynth, and MBA-Solver benchmarks, where the reported method averages about 0.1 seconds per expression against much slower GAMBA and SSPAM.

Glenside is a language for tensor programs that maps them onto matrix hardware. Each tensor is an access pattern: an outer shape of items, plus each item’s shape. Rewrites fill an e-graph with equivalent programs, and a fixed rule spots forms a systolic-array accelerator can run. ¶ This problem removes the analysis that attaches facts to each class of equal expressions: shapes, known zero regions and accelerator use. The agent writes how a fact is built from its parts’ facts, and how two facts merge when classes join. ¶ Workloads are small convolutions and concatenations feeding a dot product. To pass, on every workload it must find an exact accelerator form whenever the human reference does. It must also use no more rewrite time and add no more graph nodes.

TenSat applies equality saturation to tensor-graph superoptimization, exploring many equivalent computation graphs at once instead of the order-sensitive sequential rewrites production frameworks use. The Rust implementation builds on egg and extracts an optimal graph with an ILP solver. The task removes the saturation and extraction core, keeping the TASO-derived rewrite rules and cost model. The agent reimplements graph construction and ILP extraction. The objective is to match or beat the authors on runtime speedup and optimization time across BERT, ResNeXt-50, NasRNN, and Inception-v3 on a Tesla T4, where TenSat reaches 16 percent speedup at 48 times less time than TASO.

ACC Saturator optimizes directive-based GPU code by building single-assignment forms, rewriting them exhaustively with equality saturation, and extracting an implementation that cuts computation and memory access. The tool is written in Racket, parses OpenACC and OpenMP through XcodeML, and uses the egg library. The task removes the saturation and extraction stage that rewrites the single-assignment form. The agent reimplements this stage so the emitted kernels stay correct and fast. The objective is to match or beat the authors on execution time and memory throughput across the NAS Parallel Benchmarks and SPEC ACCEL suite on A100 GPUs under the reported compilers.

Spectre shows that speculative execution leaks memory across security boundaries by training branch predictors and reading traces through cache side channels. Variant 1 mistrains a conditional bounds check and variant 2 poisons indirect branches, with secrets recovered through Flush+Reload. The task removes the speculation-gadget and cache-probe core from the proof-of-concept. The harness and measurement scaffolding remain. The agent reimplements the training, transient access, and side-channel readout. The objective is to match the authors by leaking chosen victim memory at the reported rate of roughly 10 KB per second at under 0.01 percent error on the x86 target.

This paper argues that static evaluation overstates LLM defense robustness and that adaptive attackers tuning four optimization families, namely gradient descent, reinforcement learning, search, and human red-teaming, break defenses reported as strong. It attacks twelve jailbreak and prompt-injection defenses across HarmBench, AgentDojo, and OpenPromptInject. The task removes the adaptive attack-construction core. The evaluation harness and defense wrappers stay intact. The agent reimplements the optimization loops that craft defense-specific attacks. The objective is to match or beat the authors on attack success rate, driving most defenses above 90 percent where the original reports claimed near zero.

Progent secures AI agents through privilege control, expressing allowed tool calls as symbolic rules and confining the agent so its action space can only shrink without approval. An LLM drafts and updates policies and an SMT solver classifies each update as narrowing or expanding. The repository holds the policy engine plus the AgentDojo and ASB harnesses. The task removes the policy enforcement and monotonic-confinement core. The agent reimplements rule evaluation and the narrowing check. The objective is to match or beat the authors by cutting attack success rate and preserving task utility on AgentDojo and ASB.

Opal provides private memory for personal AI by confining semantic reasoning to trusted enclaves, so that untrusted disk sees only oblivious accesses through ORAM, backed by an in-enclave knowledge graph and continuous reindexing. The Rust protocol serves controller, embedding, and LLM enclaves over encrypted vector and chunk stores. The task removes the oblivious-access and knowledge-graph query core. The agent reimplements ORAM-backed retrieval and graph filtering. The objective is to match or beat the authors on retrieval accuracy, throughput, and cost against the ANN-only and Graphiti baselines on the synthetic personal-data corpus of 190,000 artifacts and 1,300 queries the paper reports.

This paper introduces Blind Return-Oriented Programming, which exploits a stack overflow in a remote service with no binary or source by observing whether each probe crashes. The attack locates gadgets through stack reads, builds a ROP chain, and writes out the binary to escalate. The task removes the gadget-discovery and chain-construction core. The crash-oracle harness against the server stays in place. The agent reimplements blind gadget finding and chain assembly. The objective is to match the authors by achieving remote code execution on a stack-vulnerable server within the reported few thousand requests and hours-scale time.

Diffusion Policy controls a robot by generating its moves the way image models generate pictures. It starts from random noise and removes it step by step. A trained network guides each step, using what the robot just saw. The robot makes the first few moves, then plans again. ¶ The problem removes the sampler, the loop that turns noise into moves. The trained network stays fixed. The agent writes the loop: how many denoising steps, and how each step updates the sample. The authors’ loop takes 100 steps. ¶ A simulated robot pushes a T-shaped block into place over many episodes. To pass, it must match or beat the human reference on reward and success in every group of episodes. It must also plan faster and finish the whole run sooner.

MuJoCo Playground trains robot controllers in a GPU simulator within minutes. One example teaches a Unitree Go1 quadruped to follow joystick commands. The policy reads the robot’s own sensors and the commanded speed and turn rate. It outputs target angles for the twelve joints. ¶ The problem removes nothing; the authors’ training recipe is the bar. The agent writes its own training procedure, from scratch, in the same time. It may change the rewards, training commands, pushes, terrain, network or learning algorithm. ¶ Five training runs are each tested on flat ground, under pushes and on rough terrain. Each test drives thousands of simulated robots. To pass, the policy must beat the human reference in every test on five counts. These are total reward, speed tracking, turn tracking, energy use and smoothness.

MetaOpt finds traffic on which a wide-area network heuristic falls furthest behind the optimal routing. The heuristic here keeps the better of two shortcuts. POP splits demands into three groups, each with a third of every link. Demand pinning sends each small demand along its shortest path. ¶ This problem removes the search for that traffic, and the agent writes it. For each of 27 source–destination pairs, it picks a demand of 0, 6 or 18, at most nine nonzero. Good choices defeat both shortcuts at once. ¶ Instances use three real networks with perturbed link capacities. Exact linear programs replay the demands to measure the heuristic’s gap from the optimum. To pass, on every instance the gap must be at least as large as with the human reference.

Shockwave schedules machine-learning training jobs on a shared GPU cluster. Many jobs change their batch size as they train, and with it their speed. Shockwave plans for these changes ahead, to finish jobs fast while treating each one fairly. ¶ This problem removes the policy’s decision for each round, and the agent writes it. Each round, it chooses which live jobs run, within the cluster’s four GPUs. The simulator handles the rest, from job progress to batch-size changes. ¶ Each submission schedules two traces of eight jobs. The jobs train language, vision, recommendation and translation models. To pass, it must beat the human reference on four counts in both traces. They are makespan, average job completion time, the worst slowdown against a fair share, and the fraction of unfair jobs.

BBQ is a hardware priority queue that schedules network packets by integer priority. It keeps a first-in first-out bucket per priority under a tree of bitmaps. A set bit means its subtree holds packets, so the smallest priority lies along the first set bits. ¶ The problem removes the bitmap-level logic from a program that generates the queue’s hardware. The agent writes that logic. Each level must serve enqueue, dequeue-min and dequeue-max, even when operations arrive back to back. ¶ Each design is simulated on operation traces at several tree depths, bitmap widths and capacities. Its responses must match a correct queue, and synthesis sets its clock rate. To pass, it must beat the human reference on operations per second at every configuration. Its worst response latency must be no longer.

RedTE performs distributed traffic engineering with multi-agent reinforcement learning so each router acts on local state and reaches near-centralized quality within a sub-100-millisecond control loop. The repository holds the DRLTE agents and an LP solver that computes the optimal reference. The task removes the MARL policy that outputs routing decisions. The simulator, traffic-matrix generator, and LP reference stay in place. The agent reimplements the cooperative agent training and inference. The objective is to match or beat the authors on performance ratio against the LP optimum and on control-loop latency across the GEANT and Abilene topologies the paper reports.

AWQ compresses LLMs with weight-only low-bit quantization, protecting the roughly 1 percent salient channels identified from activation statistics through per-channel scaling rather than mixed precision. The method needs no backpropagation and pairs with the TinyChat kernel runtime. The task removes the activation-aware scale-search and quantization core. Calibration and inference stay wired in. The agent reimplements salient-channel scaling and INT4 quantization. The objective is to match or beat the authors on WikiText-2 perplexity and downstream accuracy at INT4 group size 128 across LLaMA, OPT, and Mistral against the round-to-nearest and GPTQ baselines, with the reported 3-plus times speedup over FP16.

StreamingLLM enables unbounded streaming inference by keeping a few initial attention-sink tokens alongside a rolling window of recent tokens, exploiting the finding that models dump attention onto the first tokens. It needs no fine-tuning and handles millions of tokens. The task removes the sink-plus-window KV-cache management from the attention path. The model and decoding loop stay in place. The agent reimplements sink retention and cache rolling. The objective is to match the authors on stable PG19 perplexity across extended sequences and on the reported speedup of up to 22.2 times over sliding-window recomputation on Llama-2, MPT, and Falcon.

KIVI quantizes the KV cache to 2 bits without tuning, applying per-channel quantization to keys and per-token quantization to values to fit each cache's distribution. The released code integrates the asymmetric scheme into LLM inference. The task removes the quantization and dequantization kernels for both cache halves. The attention and inference path stay wired in. The agent reimplements per-channel key and per-token value quantization. The objective is to match or beat the authors on accuracy across CoQA, TruthfulQA, GSM8K, and LongBench, plus the reported 2.6 times memory reduction and up to 3.47 times throughput gain on an A100.

Hydragen speeds batched inference over shared prefixes by decomposing attention into a shared-prefix term and per-sequence suffix terms, recombining them with log-sum-exp rescaling so prefix attention batches into compute-friendly matrix products. It extends to tree-structured prompt sharing. The task removes the attention-decomposition and recombination core. The inference harness stays in place. The agent reimplements the split prefix and suffix attention and the softmax merge. The objective is to match or beat the authors on throughput with CodeLlama-13b, where Hydragen reaches up to 32 times the vLLM baseline and loses under 15 percent as the prefix grows to 16K tokens.

Wanda prunes LLMs in a single forward pass by removing weights with the smallest product of magnitude and input-activation norm, comparing per output and needing no retraining or weight update. The repository applies this across unstructured and 2:4 and 4:8 sparsity. The task removes the pruning-metric and mask-selection core. Calibration and evaluation stay wired in. The agent reimplements the activation-weighted score and per-output selection. The objective is to match or beat the authors on WikiText perplexity and zero-shot accuracy at 50 percent sparsity across LLaMA and LLaMA-2 against magnitude pruning and SparseGPT, where LLaMA-65B holds dense-level accuracy.

FastV accelerates large vision-language models by observing that image tokens receive little attention in deep layers, so it keeps full attention through early layers and prunes low-ranked visual tokens afterward. With cut layer K equal to 2 and ratio R equal to 50 percent it removes about 45 percent of FLOPs. The task removes the attention-ranking and token-pruning core. The model forward stays in place. The agent reimplements the ranking and drop. The objective is to match the authors on accuracy across A-OKVQA, MMMU, SeedBench, and video QA on LLaVA-1.5, QwenVL-Chat, and Video-LLaVA at the reported FLOP reduction.

DeepCache accelerates diffusion sampling without training by caching high-level U-Net features across adjacent denoising steps and refreshing only low-level features through the skip connections. It composes with DDIM and PLMS samplers. The task removes the feature-cache scheduling and reuse logic. The sampling loop and model stay wired in. The agent reimplements the caching interval and partial-forward reuse. The objective is to match or beat the authors on image quality and speed, where Stable Diffusion v1.5 reaches 2.3 times speedup at 0.05 CLIP-score drop and LDM-4-G on ImageNet reaches 4.1 times speedup at 0.22 FID change across the reported datasets.

Sparse VideoGen2 accelerates video diffusion by clustering tokens with k-means to reorder them by semantic similarity, which sharpens critical-token identification and densifies their layout so sparse attention wastes little GPU work. The training-free method adds top-p budget control and custom kernels. The task removes the semantic-permutation and sparse-attention core. The diffusion pipeline stays in place. The agent reimplements the clustering, reordering, and sparse attention. The objective is to match or beat the authors on PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and VBench against SVG, SpargeAttention, and XAttention, reaching up to 2.30 times and 1.89 times speedup on HunyuanVideo and Wan 2.1.

Lookahead decoding breaks the sequential dependency of autoregressive generation by trading extra parallel FLOPs to cut decoding steps, generating and verifying n-gram guesses without any draft model and staying compatible with FlashAttention. The task removes the n-gram generation and verification core. The sampling harness stays wired in. The agent reimplements the parallel lookahead and verification branch that preserves the output distribution. The objective is to match or beat the authors on latency across MT-Bench, HumanEval, GSM8K, and ClassEval with LLaMA-2-Chat and CodeLlama, reaching the reported 1.8 times speedup on MT-Bench and up to 4 times on code completion.

SliceGPT compresses transformers post-training by applying orthogonal transformations that leave the network computationally invariant, then deleting rows and columns to shrink the embedding dimension into smaller dense matrices that run on stock hardware. The task removes the invariance-transform and slicing core. Calibration and evaluation stay wired in. The agent reimplements the orthogonal rotation and principal-component slicing. The objective is to match or beat the authors on WikiText-2 perplexity and zero-shot accuracy on PIQA, WinoGrande, HellaSwag, and ARC across LLAMA-2-70B, OPT-66B, and Phi-2, retaining up to 99 percent performance at 25 percent slicing against the SparseGPT baseline.

Multiplying two sparse matrices is a core step in graph analytics and scientific computing. This paper reorders rows so that similar rows sit together. It then multiplies eight neighboring rows at once, reading each needed row of the second matrix once per group. ¶ This problem removes the clustered format and its multiply. The agent writes both. Each group of eight rows becomes one list of column ids, with eight values per id. The multiply then works cluster by cluster. ¶ Each submission multiplies real matrices from structural mechanics, numerical stencils, irregular systems and directed graphs. Results must match the authors’ arithmetic closely. To pass, it must beat the human reference by more than 15 percent in run time and throughput, on every matrix.

Stream-K parallelizes GPU GEMM by splitting the aggregate inner-loop iterations evenly across processing elements rather than assigning output tiles, removing the quantization inefficiency that idles cores on awkward problem shapes. It ships one kernel per precision inside CUTLASS. The task removes the work-decomposition and partial-tile reduction core. The tile machinery stays in place. The agent reimplements the iteration partitioning and cross-block accumulation. The objective is to match or beat the authors across 32,824 GEMM shapes on an A100, where Stream-K averages 1.23 times over CUTLASS data-parallel at FP64 and 1.63 times at mixed FP16 from a single tile size.

KAMI multiplies small matrices inside one GPU thread block, a group of threads on one processor. It brings communication-avoiding methods from distributed matrix multiplication into the block. Its warps split the work so they exchange little data, and compute on the tensor cores. ¶ This problem removes KAMI’s double-precision kernel, the code each thread block runs. The agent writes it. Each block computes A times B transposed, plus half of the old C, on its own matrices. Every output element is checked. ¶ Each workload launches thousands of blocks, each with its own matrices, in shapes from 16×16×24 to 128×64×64. To pass, the kernel must beat the human reference on throughput for every shape, by more than the measured timing noise.

MIRA is a foundation model for medical time-series forecasting that handles irregular intervals and mixed sampling rates through continuous-time rotary positional encoding, a frequency-specific mixture of experts, and a Neural-ODE extrapolation block for arbitrary timestamps. The repository trains three sizes on a clinical corpus and evaluates zero-shot. The task removes these three blocks. Training and evaluation code stay wired in. The agent reimplements the continuous-time encoding, MoE routing, and ODE extrapolation. The objective is to match or beat the authors on RMSE and MAE across MIMIC, PTB-XL, and held-out datasets, with the reported 10 and 7 percent error reductions.

Zelda is a multi-server preprocessing PIR scheme with unconditional security. The client stores hints from a one-time offline phase and the servers keep only the original database. The Go repository splits into client, server, query, and util packages, and the task removes the client-side hint generation and online lookup logic. The agent must implement those routines so every answer matches the ground truth checked against a seeded database. Scoring compares online response time and client storage with the human reference, which reports 35ms per query on a 128GB database with 1 kilobyte entries over a simulated 1Gbps link.

Private information retrieval lets a client read one database entry without the server learning which. QuarterPIR needs no public-key cryptography. The client streams the database once and keeps hints: XORs of entries in pseudorandom sets. Each lookup then needs one short request and reply. ¶ This problem leaves out the server’s request handler. The agent writes it and may redesign the messages and client. The server sees only a fixed public function of the authors’ request, so privacy is kept. ¶ Each submission serves databases of 65,536 and 67 million entries, a thousand random lookups each. Every lookup must be correct. To pass, it must send fewer bytes than the human reference on every lookup. It must also be faster in server, setup and lookup time, and use no more client memory.

Piano is a single-server PIR scheme with sublinear online computation built from pseudorandom functions rather than homomorphic encryption. The client runs a streaming setup phase and then answers each lookup in amortized work proportional to the square root of the database size. The Go repository contains the server, the client_new implementation, and configuration for entry count and width. The task removes the client's hint construction and online query routines. The agent must restore them so each retrieved entry is correct. Scoring compares query time and client storage with the human reference, which reaches 12ms per lookup on a 100GB database.

A matrix’s polar factor keeps its singular vectors but sets every singular value to one. The Muon optimizer needs it at every step, where an SVD is too slow. Polar Express instead applies a few odd polynomials, using only matrix products. Each is the best one for the range of singular values the step before leaves. ¶ The problem removes the whole method. The agent writes the best fifth-degree polynomial for a given range, and a schedule of such polynomials. It also writes the matrix iteration that applies them. ¶ Twelve square, tall and wide matrices get three to six steps each. To pass, it must beat the human reference on every matrix on five counts. They are the schedule’s worst error, three distances from the true factor, and alignment with it.

LeJEPA trains an encoder without labels: two noisy views of one hidden state should give matching outputs. A regularizer, SIGReg, pushes the outputs toward a standard Gaussian so they cannot collapse. The paper asks when this recovers the hidden state, up to a rotation. ¶ This problem removes the losses. The agent writes three: alignment between the two views, SIGReg, and whitening. None may keep state between calls. ¶ Each submission trains a small network on a toy world: a two-dimensional Gaussian state, twisted into a spiral. To pass, it must beat the human reference on six measures for each of three seeds. Two measure linear recovery of the state, in both directions. Four measure closeness to a rotation, output covariance, the alignment gap and error after the best rotation.

The Hierarchical Reasoning Model is a 27M parameter recurrent architecture with a slow high-level planner and a fast low-level module that reasons in one forward pass without chain-of-thought data or pretraining. The repository provides pretrain and evaluate scripts, dataset builders for ARC-AGI, Sudoku-Extreme, and Maze-Hard, and the model code under models. The task deletes the two-module recurrent core, its one-step gradient approximation, and the adaptive computation time halting head. The agent must implement these pieces so training runs end to end. Scoring compares exact-match accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme, Maze-Hard, ARC-AGI-1, and ARC-AGI-2 with the authors' checkpoints trained from about 1000 examples.

Mixture-of-Memories gives a linear sequence model several independent memory states and a router that sends each token to a subset of them, which raises capacity and reduces interference at unchanged complexity. The repository implements MoM layers on the Hugging Face stack with training scripts and evaluation harnesses for commonsense and recall-intensive tasks. The task removes the routed layer, including the router, per-state updates, and the shared memory. The agent must implement the layer so models train from scratch. Scoring compares accuracy on FDA, SWDE, SQuAD, NQ, TriviaQA, and DROP at 380M parameters and 15B tokens against the authors' runs.

A world model is a learned simulator: given a frame and a list of actions, it predicts the frames that follow. NanoWM uses a diffusion model on compressed images. Each future frame starts as noise, which the model removes step by step, guided by the actions. Each frame has its own noise level, so some can finish before others. ¶ The problem removes the sampler that drives this process. The agent writes the schedule of noise levels per frame and step, and the update between levels. The trained model stays fixed. ¶ Each submission predicts three future frames of a point moving through a simulated maze. To pass, on every clip it must beat the human reference on signal-to-noise ratio, structural similarity and a learned perceptual distance.

DFlash accelerates LLM decoding with a lightweight block diffusion drafter that proposes many tokens in one forward pass from hidden features of the target model, which then verifies the proposal in parallel. The repository holds the dflash package with drafter definition, feature extraction, and generation loops for Transformers, MLX, and server backends, plus benchmark scripts. The task removes the drafter and its verification loop. The agent must implement both so outputs stay identical to greedy decoding of the target. Scoring compares speedup and accepted tokens per step on GSM8K, MATH500, HumanEval, MBPP, and MT-Bench with Qwen3-8B against the authors' drafter.

RAGEN trains language models with reinforcement learning to act over many turns. The model sees a puzzle, replies with moves, then gets the next view and a reward. Training needs these games packed into token batches that mark what to learn from. ¶ The problem removes the context manager that does this, and the agent writes it. It builds each prompt from the real history and parses replies into moves. It packs whole games into padded rows, with masks and with each reward on the right token. Games from the same start stay in one group. ¶ Each run plays Sokoban, a box-pushing puzzle, with a small model, then takes one training step. To pass, every group of games must beat the human reference on both puzzles solved and average reward.

JiT trains a plain large-patch Transformer on raw pixels to output the clean image instead of noise or velocity, which lets pixel-space diffusion succeed at patch sizes of 16 and 32 without a tokenizer or auxiliary loss. The repository contains model_jit.py, engine_jit.py, denoiser.py, a training entry point, and FID reference statistics. The task removes the clean-image head and the denoiser that converts its output into a flow for sampling. The agent must implement both so training and sampling run at 256 and 512 resolution. Scoring compares FID and Inception Score over 50,000 generated ImageNet samples with the authors' checkpoints.

Transformers normalize their activations with LayerNorm, which computes a mean and a variance at every layer. The DyT paper replaces it with one element-wise function, γ · tanh(αx) + β, where α is learned. Models train as well without the statistics. ¶ This problem removes DyT and the routine that swaps it in. The agent writes both: the layer, with its own α, γ and β at each site, and a conversion that leaves no LayerNorm in the model. ¶ The model is a Vision Transformer, trained briefly from scratch on small sets of flower photos. Its outputs and gradients must stay close to those of the authors’ layer. To pass, its accuracy must be at least the authors’, and both training and inference must be faster.

CLIPPO trains one Vision Transformer on photographs and on text rendered as pixels with a contrastive loss, so a single encoder handles retrieval, zero-shot classification, and language understanding with half the parameters of CLIP. The code lives in the big_vision repository under configs/proj/clippo with a training config, README, and demo notebook. The task removes the text rendering preprocessing op and the shared-encoder contrastive model definition. The agent must implement them so the config trains end to end. Scoring compares zero-shot ImageNet classification accuracy and image-text retrieval recall with the numbers recorded in the authors' config comments.

The paper shows that sparse Mixture-of-Experts models degrade faster than dense Transformers when training data repeats, with 80M active parameter MoEs suffering at 4 repetitions where their counterparts tolerate 8. It then finds that dropout and masking-based regularization let MoEs beat the baseline past 64 repetitions. No repository is listed, so the task builds on the training stack the authors describe with OLMoE-style data. The task removes the data repetition scheduler and the expert output masking regularizer. The agent must implement both so sweeps over repetition rate run. Scoring compares held-out cross-entropy on the validation domains against the authors' curves.

Agentic Context Engineering improves an LLM system by evolving its prompt as a structured playbook instead of updating weights. A generator produces trajectories, a reflector extracts lessons, and a curator merges them as delta updates with helpful and harmful counters. The repository holds the ace package with these three roles plus evaluation scripts for AppWorld, FiNER, and XBRL Formula. The task removes the reflector and curator, including the deterministic merge logic. The agent must implement them so offline and online adaptation run. Scoring compares AppWorld success and finance accuracy with the authors' reported gains of 10.6 and 8.6 points.

Meta Context Engineering makes prompt optimization learnable with a bi-level system. A meta-level agent refines engineering skills through agentic crossover over the history of executions, and a base-level agent runs the current skill to turn training rollouts into context stored as files and code. The repository provides mce with meta_agent.py and base_agent.py, task environments under env, and scripts for finance, chemistry, medicine, law, and AI safety. The task removes the meta-level agent and its crossover search. The agent must implement it so skills improve across iterations. Scoring compares accuracy on the five domains with the authors' offline and online results.

Meta-Harness optimizes the harness around a language model with an agentic proposer that reads the source code, scores, and execution traces of every earlier candidate. The repository ships two reference examples, a memory-system search for online text classification and a scaffold evolution for Terminal-Bench 2, with a Claude Code wrapper as the default proposer. The task deletes the outer optimization loop that stages candidates, scores them, and exposes the history. The agent must implement the loop so searches run. Scoring compares the best discovered harness with the authors' result of a 7.7 point classification gain at 4x fewer context tokens.

Self-Harness lets a model improve its own agent scaffold. The loop mines weaknesses from execution traces, proposes minimal harness edits tied to those failures, and accepts an edit only after held-in and held-out regression checks pass. The repository contains diagnosis, proposer, acceptance, workflow, and eval directories plus a released Qwen harness. The task removes the weakness mining and proposal modules. The agent must implement them so the loop yields validated edits. Scoring compares Terminal-Bench 2.0 pass rate after self-improvement with the authors' runs, which lift Qwen3.5-35B-A3B from 18.0 to 36.7 and MiniMax M2.5 from 42.2 to 53.9 percent.

SemJoin optimizes semantic joins, which match rows across tables on a natural-language predicate. An LLM advisor routes each query to a classifier strategy for predicates over a discrete label set or to a cluster join that embeds rows, groups both tables, and prunes group pairs by sampling. The repository provides advisor.py, classifier_join.py, cluster_join.py, and evaluation scripts for three datasets. The task removes the advisor and the cluster join with its pruning step. The agent must implement them, and scoring compares F1 and token cost on IMDb reviews, emails, and Stack Overflow tags with the authors' results.

Regions Sort is a parallel radix sort that works in place. It groups keys by their top eight bits, then sorts each group by the rest. After counting, each bucket’s final interval is known, and misplaced elements form a graph between buckets. ¶ The problem removes the part that plans moves on this region graph, and the agent writes it. It turns edges into swaps of equal-length ranges. It hands out rounds of swaps that do not overlap, then updates the graph. ¶ Each submission sorts twelve arrays of 2.4 to 16 million keys or key–payload pairs: uniform, skewed, repeated or nearly sorted. To pass, it must beat the human reference on sort time and on region-graph time for every array. Its extra memory must stay within 5% of the input.

DBSCAN finds clusters as dense regions and marks isolated points as noise. A point is core if enough points lie within distance ε of it. Core points within ε of each other share a cluster. This paper makes exact DBSCAN fast in parallel by bucketing points into grid cells. ¶ This problem removes the step that links core points into clusters, and the agent writes it. It must find which neighboring cells hold core points within ε of each other. Then it gives every core point a cluster id. ¶ Each submission clusters generated sets of 12,000 to 200,000 points in three to seven dimensions. Its output must match an exact reference point by point. To pass, it must beat the human reference on running time for every point set.

A hypergraph lets one edge join any number of vertices. Core numbers show how deep inside its dense part each vertex sits. They come from peeling: remove every vertex in fewer than k edges, drop each edge that loses a member, and repeat. A vertex’s core number is the largest k it survives. Hygra computes them in parallel. ¶ The problem removes the core-number computation. The agent writes all of it, given each vertex’s edges and each edge’s vertices. Every core number must be exact. ¶ Each submission runs on random hypergraphs with hundreds of thousands of vertices and millions of memberships. To pass, on every hypergraph it must beat the human reference by at least 3%, on eight threads and on one.

A butterfly is two vertices on each side of a bipartite graph, joined by all four edges. Counting them measures how tightly the graph clusters, much as triangle counting does. ParButterfly counts them in parallel. It finds wedges, paths of two edges, and groups them by their endpoints. ¶ This problem removes the routine that counts every butterfly in a graph. The agent writes it for four threads, and the count must be exact. It may choose its own vertex order and way of grouping wedges. ¶ The eight test graphs have about two million edges each. Six have uniform degrees; two have heavily skewed degrees on both sides. To pass, it must run more than 5% faster than the authors’ parallel code on every graph.

ConnectIt is a framework for parallel connected components that combines k-out, BFS, and LDD sampling with union-find linking and compression schemes to produce several hundred algorithm variants, and it also supports incremental edge insertions. The code lives in the gbbs repository under benchmarks/Connectivity/ConnectIt with framework.h, sampling.h, and per-variant mains. The task removes the sampling strategies and the finish phase that unites the remaining edges. The agent must implement them so every variant returns correct labels. Scoring compares running time on the paper's graphs against the human reference, which reports an average 12.4x speedup over prior multicore algorithms on 72 cores.

FARGO finds the vectors with the largest inner product with a query, without checking them all. It hashes each vector into several tables, one bit per random projection. It probes the closest buckets across all tables at once. It stops when better answers become unlikely. ¶ This problem removes the query core, and the agent writes it. The core streams buckets from all tables, each listed once. Each carries its distance from the query: the sum of squared projections on the bits that differ. The core also decides when to stop. ¶ Searches run on two datasets from the paper, Audio and MNIST, at twelve settings. To pass, every setting must equal or beat the human reference on recall and answer quality. It must also verify no more candidates and answer faster.

short: Binary Fuse Filter Construction and Lookup
description: A binary fuse filter tells whether a key belongs to a fixed set. It never misses a stored key and rarely accepts an absent one. A lookup reads three slots of one array and XORs them. It accepts the key if the result equals the key’s fingerprint, a short hash. ¶ This problem removes construction, the step that fills the array. The agent writes it for 8-bit and 16-bit fingerprints, so every stored key’s three slots XOR to its fingerprint. It may also reshape the filter and its lookup. ¶ Filters hold 10,000 to 1,000,000 keys and answer streams with different shares of stored keys. To pass, every workload must beat the human reference on memory, construction time and lookup time. The false-positive rate and space overhead must not be measurably worse.

An image tokenizer turns a photo into latent tokens and decodes them back. DeTok trains the tokenizer as a denoiser: it hides most image patches and adds noise to the latents. The decoder must still rebuild the clean image. ¶ This problem removes that corruption. The agent chooses which patches to hide and how to add noise to the latents. It also decides what fills each hidden position, so the decoder gets a full sequence in order. Evaluation stays clean. ¶ Each workload briefly continues training on a small photo set and reconstructs others. To pass, the model and a running average of its weights must both beat the human reference on every workload. They are scored by PSNR, a standard measure of pixel accuracy. The whole run must also finish sooner.

Contreap is an ordered index built on a treap, a binary search tree balanced by random priorities. Each transaction makes a new version, and every past version stays readable. Nodes store subtree counts, so range sums are fast. ¶ This problem removes the update scheduler and the update routines. The agent writes them: insert and delete on several threads, publishing one complete tree per transaction. A reader may ask for any version at any moment and must never see a half-built tree. ¶ Traces of about half a million inserts, deletes and range queries run on four to six threads. To pass, every case and thread setting must beat the human reference on three counts. These are throughput, peak memory and the time of range queries on past versions.

Fréchet distance compares two image sets by the mean and covariance of their features. This paper turns it into a training loss for image generators. Its statistics must cover many generated images, yet pass gradients to the current batch. ¶ This problem removes the feature queue that holds these statistics, and the agent writes it. It keeps past features or running estimates of their mean and covariance. It mixes in each new batch so gradients reach it, without keeping old computation graphs. ¶ Each workload post-trains the authors’ released generator on a short schedule. Fresh images are then scored in six feature spaces, including Inception, DINOv2 and CLIP. To pass, the normalized Fréchet distance must be lower than with the human reference in all six spaces, on every workload.

FARGO finds the stored vectors whose dot product with a query is largest. Retrieval and recommendation systems depend on this search. FARGO groups vectors by length and hashes each group into several tables. It probes buckets across all the tables in one global order. ¶ The problem removes the rule that ends this probing. The agent writes it: after each bucket, decide whether more probes could still improve the answer. It may use a lookup table the authors computed in advance. ¶ Queries come from a real audio dataset, under three accuracy settings and four result-list sizes. To pass, it must beat the human reference at every setting. Its queries must be faster and its recall no lower. Its last result must be no worse, and it must check no more vectors.

JoinBoost trains gradient-boosted trees inside a database, using only SQL. The data stay in normalized tables: a large table of sales and small ones for items, stores and dates. It never builds their join, and only small aggregates leave the database. ¶ The problem removes the residual update that follows each tree. Each tree fits the error earlier trees leave, stored in the sales table. The agent writes the update: each sales row subtracts its leaf’s scaled value. Finding that leaf can need other tables’ columns. ¶ Training runs on one to two million real grocery sales, over three join layouts. The model must match one trained on the fully joined table. To pass, it must beat the human reference on every case, in both training time and update time.

CKKS is a homomorphic encryption scheme: it computes on encrypted vectors of complex numbers. Each operation adds a little noise, so results are only approximately right. The paper’s estimator predicts how many bits of precision survive. It replays the computation on clear values, adding modeled noise at each step. ¶ The problem removes seven of the estimator’s kernels: the noise of multiplication, summed products, rescaling, division with rounding and key switching. The agent writes them and may redesign how the estimator represents a noisy value. ¶ Each submission predicts nine encrypted computations, from one product to bootstrapping, under 29 settings. Real encrypted runs give the true mean and spread of precision. To pass, on every setting it must predict both as well as the human reference, and run faster.

Edlib computes the exact edit distance between two DNA strings, and an alignment that achieves it. The alignment is a path through a table with one cell per pair of positions. Edlib recovers the path without storing the table, by Hirschberg’s method. It finds where an optimal path crosses the middle row, then solves each half the same way. ¶ The problem removes this path recovery. The agent writes it back, given the two strings and their exact distance. Any optimal path of matches, mismatches, insertions and deletions is accepted. ¶ Each submission aligns DNA pairs of 10,000 and 30,000 bases, 60% to 99% similar, in three alignment modes. To pass, on every pair its path recovery must be faster than the human reference and use no more memory.

A branch predictor guesses which way each conditional branch will go, before the processor knows. Each wrong guess wastes work on the wrong path. RUNLTS predicts from past branches, and also from register values once the instructions producing them have run. ¶ The problem removes the register-value part of its statistical corrector, a stage that adjusts the main guess. The agent writes it. It must track values as instructions run out of order, and never trust a value a newer instruction replaces. It turns them into a vote on each branch, within a fixed storage limit. ¶ Each submission runs a cycle-level simulator over 105 program traces. To pass, on every trace it must make fewer mispredictions than the human reference and lose fewer wrong-path cycles.

Flow-OPD teaches an image model to render the words a prompt asks for. A flow-matching model makes an image by moving noise through a chain of latent states. The student draws its own chains, and a teacher tuned for text supervises each step. ¶ The problem removes the trajectory sampler and the step function it calls. The agent writes both. The sampler runs the student from noise to image and records every state. The step draws the next state and scores it with a Gaussian log-probability, which replay must reproduce. ¶ The student is Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium, trained briefly on prompts that quote the text to draw. Optical character recognition then reads held-out images. To pass, each must score higher than with the human reference, unless both are already perfect.
